finale.title: Port Jefferson Ferry
finale.subtitle: Long Island Sound crossing to Bridgeport, Connecticut
finale.closingLine: Nine pieces of the harbor — one ferry still ties Long Island to Connecticut.

checkpoints.name: Ferry Terminal
checkpoints.blurb: The Bridgeport & Port Jefferson ferry terminal is the village’s living bridge across Long Island Sound — scheduled boats still tie New York’s north shore to Connecticut.
facts: Terminal address area: West Broadway at the harbor.
The route connects Port Jefferson, NY with Bridgeport, CT.
For many visitors, the ferry is Port Jeff: arrival, departure, and skyline in one glance.

checkpoints.name: Shipbuilders Memorial
checkpoints.blurb: Harborfront Park’s landmark sculpture shows shipbuilders carrying a hull frame toward the water — a public honor to the yards that built Port Jefferson’s name.
facts: The park occupies waterfront land that once held heavy industry, including oil terminal use before civic conversion.
The sculpture is the emotional centerpiece of the harbor lawn and pier district.
Shipbuilding east of Brooklyn once made Port Jefferson a serious maritime workplace, not only a postcard harbor.

checkpoints.name: Bayles Shipyard
checkpoints.blurb: Bayles Shipyard is listed on the National Register of Historic Places — chandlery, machine shop, and mould loft from an era when hulls, not boutiques, defined this shore.
facts: Key surviving industrial buildings date to the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
Wartime and commercial work passed through these yards before later reuse.
The machine shop / mould loft fabric later supported civic harbor life (Village Center area).

checkpoints.name: Village Center
checkpoints.blurb: The Village Center turns former shipyard space into a public harbor hub — programming and gathering where industry once dominated.
facts: Civic reuse is part of Port Jeff’s modern waterfront identity.
Standing here links memorial lawn, yards, and ferry traffic in one walk.

checkpoints.name: Historical Society Museum
checkpoints.blurb: The Mather House Museum complex is the village’s attic: shipwright tools, clocks, shops, and sail-loft memory kept by the Historical Society of Greater Port Jefferson.
facts: The Mather House (mid-19th century) was home to a shipbuilding family and later tied to the Mather hospital bequest story.
Outbuildings interpret trades and everyday village commerce.
A harbor diorama / maritime collections help visitors see the waterfront before today’s park.

checkpoints.name: Main Street
checkpoints.blurb: Main Street is the everyday village spine between the hills and the harbor — shops and sidewalks framing how most visitors first meet downtown Port Jefferson.
facts: The corridor connects residential hills to the working waterfront.
Storefronts and inns give the village its walkable character beyond the ferry postcard.

checkpoints.name: Waterfront Dining
checkpoints.blurb: Harbor dining is part of Port Jeff’s welcome — tables facing the same water the ferry crosses.
facts: Waterfront restaurants and inns cluster along the Broadway harbor edge.
This pin marks a dining zone, not a single branded venue.

checkpoints.name: Drowned Meadow Cottage Museum
checkpoints.blurb: Drowned Meadow Cottage remembers an earlier landscape before the modern downtown filled the meadow.
facts: A compact museum stop that deepens the village story beyond the postcard harbor.
The name recalls the meadow that once sat where later streets and fill reshaped the shore.

checkpoints.name: Harbor Overlook
checkpoints.blurb: From the overlook, Long Island Sound opens — the path the ferry still takes to Connecticut.
facts: Sightlines across the harbor reconnect park, shipyard memory, and the ferry route.
This stop closes the walk with the same water that opens the finale.
